candidato.titulo: Study shows a small change in dialysis mortality calculations could have big impacts for patient care
candidato.resumo: A dialysis center that receives a poor mortality rating one year could receive a better rating the next, even if nothing about its patient care has changed. That is one potential consequence of a recent change in how Medicare collects patient information, according to a new analysis led by researchers at Brown University's School of Public Health and Warren Alpert Medical School and published in JAMA Internal Medicine.

texto_fonte:
Study shows a small change in dialysis mortality calculations could have big impacts for patient care
A dialysis center that receives a poor mortality rating one year could receive a better rating the next, even if nothing about its patient care has changed. That is one potential consequence of a recent change in how Medicare collects patient information, according to a new analysis led by researchers at Brown University's School of Public Health and Warren Alpert Medical School and published in JAMA Internal Medicine.
The change happened in July 2025 when U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services officials stopped collecting race and ethnicity information across several federal forms, including one completed when patients begin treatment for kidney failure. The data on race and ethnicity are among numerous social and medical factors used in a formula that helps the Medicare system evaluate dialysis centers, where patients with kidney failure receive lifesaving treatment that filters their blood.
It is not yet clear how Medicare will calculate future mortality ratings without that information or when the removal of race and ethnicity data might affect the ratings patients see, but researchers used historical data to understand what those changes could mean.
The team simulated the removal of race and ethnicity from mortality calculations and determined that the shift could significantly alter how dialysis centers are rated on patient mortality by making many look better on paper—particularly those that serve large numbers of Black patients and/or socially disadvantaged patients.
For example, the simulation found that 27% of centers serving the highest proportions of Black patients moved into a better-performing category when race and ethnicity were removed. At the same time, nearly 22% of centers serving the most socially disadvantaged patients also improved their rankings, while about 15% of centers that serve fewer patients from populations facing social or economic disadvantages received worse rankings.
"Our study suggests that the removal of race and ethnicity data is going to have a significant impact on a number of dialysis facilities and how they're being scored in this model, so we wanted people to understand that going forward," said Kalli Koukounas Green, lead author of the new study and a research scientist at Brown's Department of Health Services, Policy and Practice. "A patient might see these new mortality ratings and make their referral decision based on that, not knowing that the more favorable rating is due to a modeling change."
The researchers believe the findings are particularly relevant for doctors who use these ratings to make referrals, as well as for the dialysis facilities themselves, which may use the ratings as a guide for investing in quality improvement efforts.
"These mortality measures and these kinds of relative performance rankings for dialysis facilities are important and have high-stakes consequences," said the study's senior author, Dr. Amal Trivedi, a professor of health services, policy and practice and of medicine.
How calculations can affect care
The research team examined data from 6,895 dialysis centers nationwide between 2017 and 2020. They calculated how each center would be rated based on patient death rates, first using race and ethnicity information and then leaving it out.
Centers serving more patients facing social or economic disadvantages generally received worse ratings when race and ethnicity were included in the calculations. When that information was removed, the gap in ratings between those centers and centers serving fewer disadvantaged patients nearly disappeared.
The study included some limitations, including that researchers used older data to estimate how mortality ratings might change because the effects of Medicare's new data collection practices are not yet known. Researchers said future research should examine how much dialysis center ratings actually change once the new practices are reflected in Medicare's published ratings.
The findings also point to a larger issue across health care of how changes in government data collection can affect important health care decisions. Hospitals, nursing homes and other medical providers, for example, are also evaluated using quality ratings that patients and families may rely on when making decisions. As in this study, changes to how those ratings are calculated could make providers appear better or worse without reflecting actual differences in care.
"It's important for federal policymakers to be aware that when you change health data collection, it affects our ability to understand public health trends and measure clinical performance," Trivedi said.
Publication details
Kalli G. Koukounas et al., Removing Race From Standardized Mortality Ratio Risk Adjustment in Dialysis Care Quality Measurement, JAMA Internal Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.1001/jamainternmed.2026.5632
Journal information: JAMA Internal Medicine

candidato.titulo: DNA reveals the secret lives of Hawaiʻi's aeʻo (Hawaiian stilt)
candidato.resumo: Long-legged, tuxedo-clad and famously noisy, the aeʻo, or Hawaiian stilt (Himantopus mexicanus knudseni), has a family life as complicated as any reality TV show. A new study led by University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa researchers, published in Ecology and Evolution, paired a decade of birdwatching with DNA sequencing to uncover a world of egg-dumping, secret infidelities and surprisingly close family ties among the newly downlisted species.

texto_fonte:
DNA reveals the secret lives of Hawaiʻi's aeʻo (Hawaiian stilt)
Long-legged, tuxedo-clad and famously noisy, the aeʻo, or Hawaiian stilt (Himantopus mexicanus knudseni), has a family life as complicated as any reality TV show. A new study led by University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa researchers, published in Ecology and Evolution, paired a decade of birdwatching with DNA sequencing to uncover a world of egg-dumping, secret infidelities and surprisingly close family ties among the newly downlisted species.
Finding clues
Aeʻo usually nest in pairs, but researchers observed unusual family arrangements, including three adults sharing a nest and multiple generations defending territories together.
Co-author Arleone Dibben-Young color-banded more than 250 stilts on Molokaʻi and tracked them weekly for a decade. Researchers from the UH Mānoa Hawaiʻi Institute of Marine Biology and the College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resilience's (CTAHR) Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Management (NREM) analyzed DNA from 91 birds to investigate their family relationships.
One incubating female was not the chick's genetic mother. This was the first genetic confirmation of "egg-dumping" in a stilt species, in which a female lays an egg in another bird's nest. Several nest "siblings" were found to be unrelated, and one mated pair may be siblings. Only about half the family ties seen in the field held up genetically.
The dangers of inbreeding
"In most bird studies, DNA sorts out parents, siblings and unrelated birds cleanly. Here, so many birds share so much ancestry that a parent and a sibling can look nearly identical," said Robert Toonen, a geneticist at HIMB. "That difficulty is itself a warning sign of how inbred this population has become."
The findings come months after the aeʻo was federally downlisted from endangered to threatened. It remains listed as endangered at the state level, with fewer than 1,800 stilts statewide.
"Downlisting is something to celebrate, but it's not the finish line," said lead author Melissa Price, a professor and wildlife ecologist at NREM. "We need to continue restoring habitat to support growing populations."
"The federal downlisting of the aeʻo reflects years of partnership among agencies, landowners and communities, and studies like this one help us see what comes next," said Afsheen Siddiqi, state waterbird biologist with the Hawaiʻi Department of Land and Natural Resources, Division of Forestry and Wildlife. "Knowing how closely related our stilts are will help us decide where to restore wetlands and how to keep these populations growing into the future."
Publication details
Melissa R. Price et al., Breeding Behaviors and Kinship in the Endangered Hawaiian Stilt (Ae'o; Himantopus mexicanus knudseni ), Ecology and Evolution (2026). DOI: 10.1002/ece3.74297

candidato.titulo: Rockwell Automation acquiring mobile robot maker AGILOX
candidato.resumo: Rockwell Automation has agreed to acquire autonomous mobile robot developer AGILOX, expanding its mobile robotics portfolio following its 2023 acquisition of OTTO Motors. The post Rockwell Automation acquiring mobile robot maker AGILOX appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
Rockwell Automation has signed a definitive agreement to acquire AGILOX, an Austria-based developer of autonomous mobile robots (AMRs). Rockwell said the acquisition will more than double the size of its AMR business and complement its existing OTTO Motors portfolio.
Financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. The deal is expected to close in the second quarter of Rockwell’s fiscal 2027, subject to regulatory approval. AGILOX will become part of Rockwell’s Intelligent Devices operating segment.
AGILOX said it has deployed more than 2,500 AMRs worldwide since its founding in 2017. The company has more than 250 employees and operations in Europe, North America, and China. Its robots are used in automotive, third-party logistics, food and beverage, and pharmaceutical applications.
The acquisition will combine OTTO’s strong presence in North America with AGILOX’s established customer base in Europe, Rockwell said.
The acquisition also marks an exit for global investment firm Carlyle, which made a majority growth investment in AGILOX in 2021. According to Carlyle, AGILOX has quadrupled its revenue since then and launched a robots-as-a-service (RaaS) offering.
How AGILOX and OTTO Motors compare
Both AGILOX and OTTO Motors develop AMRs that automate material transport. However, there are several differences between their technologies.
OTTO specializes in flatbed AMRs that can be equipped with attachments such as conveyors and lift tables to transport different materials. Its largest AMR, the OTTO 1500, can carry payloads of up to 1,900 kg (4,189 lb.). The company also offers an autonomous forklift called OTTO Lifter.
AGILOX specializes in AMRs with integrated lifting mechanisms for transporting pallets and other loads. Its robots feature omnidirectional drives, enabling them to move sideways and diagonally without turning. This allows the robots to maneuver in tight spaces. AGILOX also has an autonomous forklift.
Rockwell said the technologies are complementary, but it did not disclose how it plans to integrate the two platforms or whether customers will eventually be able to operate AGILOX and OTTO robots as part of the same fleet.
Rockwell continues to expand its robotics business
The AGILOX deal comes three years after Rockwell acquired Clearpath Robotics, including its industrial division, OTTO Motors. Rockwell valued that acquisition at $609 million at the time of purchase.
Founded in 2009 in Ontario, Canada, Clearpath initially developed mobile robots for research applications. It launched OTTO Motors in 2015 to automate material handling in industrial environments.
Rockwell has also invested in robotics beyond AMRs. In March 2025, it made a strategic investment in RightHand Robotics, a Massachusetts-based developer of robotic piece-picking systems for warehouses. Financial terms of that investment were not disclosed. RightHand Robotics combines AI, machine vision, and robotic gripping to pick individual items in fulfillment operations.

texto_fonte:
NGINX2Root: Remote Code Execution vulnerabilities in nginx
Xint is reporting that it has discovered a collection of five critical vulnerabilities in the NGINX web server. The worst flaw, it says, would allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands on an affected nginx server with HTTP/2 enabled. The company also reports a local-privilege escalation (LPE) kernel vulnerability, which was introduced in the 4.15 kernel, in the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) subsystem. If chained with the NGINX vulnerability, it would allow an attacker to gain root privileges on the host. A kernel patch for this is not yet available.
We also obtained a root shell on the host in a setup where nginx was running in
a Docker container. On many Linux distributions, the SCTP module is installed by
default and the kernel loads it automatically the first time a program opens an
SCTP socket. Whether SCTP is reachable on a given host still depends on the
kernel, the available modules, and the container's restrictions. Where it is
reachable, the attacker can take over the host kernel. Since all containers on
the host share that kernel, this gives the attacker control of the host and
every container on it.
Xint recommends updating to NGINX 1.31.9, which was just released, and to block the SCTP module on hosts that do not need it until a kernel fix is available. See the mitigations section of their report for more information.

candidato.titulo: Nvidia descarta volta de Jensen Huang ao cargo de CEO
candidato.resumo: Presidente do conselho afirmou que a empresa não pretende reconduzir o cofundador. Nvidia descarta volta de Jensen Huang ao cargo de CEO

texto_fonte:
Resumo IA
- Nvidia descartou reconduzir Jensen Huang ao cargo de CEO após sua renúncia em 12 de novembro.
- Cofundador afirmou que aceitaria voltar ao comando, caso o conselho considerasse a decisão adequada.
- Colette Kress permanece como CEO interina enquanto a empresa procura um substituto definitivo.
A Nvidia descartou reconduzir seu cofundador e ex-CEO, Jensen Huang, ao comando da fabricante de chips. Durante uma reunião com investidores na terça-feira (17/11), o presidente do conselho de administração, Harvey Jones, afirmou que a saída do executivo foi aceita por unanimidade.
Jones também disse que a empresa não responderia a perguntas sobre a renúncia nem sobre a investigação interna em andamento. A declaração foi feita poucos dias após a saída de Huang.
Jensen Huang aceitaria voltar ao comando
A declaração ocorre após Huang manifestar interesse em voltar à liderança da companhia, que ajudou a fundar em 1993. Sua saída, anunciada em 12 de novembro, aconteceu em meio às suspeitas de uma possível operação de espionagem estrangeira.
Entre os episódios investigados está um suposto relacionamento com a ex-executiva da Megaspeed, Alice Huang. A empresa é alvo de uma investigação nos Estados Unidos por suspeitas de envolvimento em operações para contornar as restrições americanas à exportação de chips para a China. As suspeitas ainda não foram comprovadas, e não há confirmação de que informações sigilosas tenham sido compartilhadas.
Ontem, Huang publicou uma mensagem no X reconhecendo ter cometido erros pessoais e afirmando que cooperaria com a investigação conduzida pelo conselho da Nvidia. O executivo também declarou que se sentiria honrado em reassumir o cargo.
Desde sua saída, executivos e funcionários do setor têm defendido a recondução de Huang ao cargo. A mobilização recebeu apoio de Elon Musk e do CEO da Epic Games, Tim Sweeney. O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, também se manifestou favoravelmente à possibilidade de retorno.
Apesar da pressão de empresários e apoiadores, o conselho mantém a decisão de não reconduzir Huang ao cargo.
Colette Kress segue como CEO interina
A diretora financeira da Nvidia, Colette Kress, assumiu interinamente a presidência da empresa e continuará acumulando as duas funções até a escolha de um sucessor. Apesar da crise de liderança, a companhia apresentou resultados trimestrais acima das expectativas do mercado.
Durante a reunião com investidores, Kress procurou transmitir confiança na continuidade das operações e afirmou que a equipe executiva está preparada para conduzir a companhia durante a transição.

candidato.titulo: NASA Data Clinches First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger
candidato.resumo: Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the Sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star at the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially “rejuvenated” star Bao. Their NASA-funded discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA’s James Webb […]

texto_fonte:
Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the Sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star at the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially “rejuvenated” star Bao. Their NASA-funded discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope that were carefully cross-referenced with extensive data from telescopes in space and on the ground.
“Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,” said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a new paper in Nature published Wednesday and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. “However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars’ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope’s data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.”
Image: AT 2025abao in the Andromeda Galaxy
Before their transformation, the two stars spent millennia placidly orbiting one another as a binary pair. But once the smaller star came into contact with the surface of the giant star, their “unification” happened after only seven orbits (about seven years). Other known binary star mergers, featuring two smaller stars, occurred after thousands of orbits.
“We thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,” said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. “One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!”
“When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect — a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao’s data,” said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. “As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star’s outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.”
This is the beginning of a high-stakes showdown some binary stars go through, known as a common envelope evolution. The gas between the stars at this stage is known as a common envelope because its outer layer is shared between them. In this system, the primary star engulfed the smaller star and the companion plummeted, spiraling through the envelope as it was robbed of orbital energy by drag. While Webb’s data proved the stars merged, a merger wasn’t the only possible outcome for this system.
In other systems, both stars survive the process — shedding a lot of mass along the way, but remaining independent in tight orbits. Over time, such surviving pairs can transform into neutron stars and black holes, explode as supernovae, produce ripples in space-time known as gravitational waves, and create millisecond pulsars.
Hitting “replay”
The team reconstructed what happened to Bao by updating their ongoing simulations. They found the model that matched Webb’s mid-infrared observations, which detailed the dust shed by the more massive primary star over centuries.
The team concluded that prior to the eruption, Bao’s primary star dwarfed the Sun: It was seven times as massive, 350 times the radius, and 18,000 times brighter — making “Big Bao” an appropriate nickname.
“It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,” said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.
Their modeling resulted in the first mass estimate for the smaller, now demolished, companion. Compared to our Sun, they found that “Little Bao” was likely less massive (about 0.7 solar masses), with a slightly smaller radius and fainter.
After revealing the masses of the pair, the model showed there might be leftover energy for Little Bao to “flee” the scene. However, further analysis determined that Little Bao was dragged into Big Bao's core. Their encounter was “almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star,” De said.
What does the new star — now simply Bao — look like today? Only future observations will identify how its “heft” settles.
Image: Andromeda Star Merger (Artist's Concept)
Reconstructing what happened
While Webb’s data allowed the team to measure how much mass was ejected during this process and how efficient the process of common envelope evolution was, Karambelkar’s team also used observations that span ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light from several telescopes to watch the events, often as they unfolded. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.)
Bao first caught the team’s attention in February 2023, when they saw an unusual variable star in data from NASA’s retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission. Before 2018, the object had a consistent luminosity. Observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) in September 2024 showed that Bao was not only beginning to brighten, but also spew dust.
When NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) serendipitously saw Bao fade rapidly in visible light and brighten in infrared light during a routine survey in July 2025, the researchers knew it was an indicator of unusual activity. The Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption on Oct. 17, 2025, watching the stars rapidly brighten and radically heat up.
In November 2025, the team received fast-turn observations from NASA’s now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab’s Gemini North telescope in Hawaii. Webb’s observations were taken on Dec. 24, 2025, as part of a just-in-time Director’s Discretionary Time program.
New path for future research
The team’s analysis of Bao, formally known as AT 2025abao, offers an approach to reconstructing the events: They conducted their analysis and made observations of the stars’ merger in real time. That allowed them to measure how efficient common envelope evolution is. In other cases, astronomers have worked to carefully reverse-engineer events that may have happened hundreds or even millions of years ago.
The new finding comes about just as NASA’s recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is about to conduct vast publicly available surveys. Its Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey will yield a huge number of new transient events that could benefit from similar analyses. “There’s going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead,” Karambelkar said.
This work is funded in part by a grant from NASA’s Astrophysics Data Analysis Program.
The James Webb Space Telescope is the largest and most powerful observatory ever sent to space, serving thousands of astronomers worldwide. Webb is solving mysteries in our solar system, looking beyond to distant worlds around other stars, and probing the mysterious structures and origins of our universe and our place in it. Webb is an international program led by NASA with its partners, ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

candidato.titulo: QuEra Computing and Berkeley Lab Publish Nature Study of Quantum Dynamics on Up to 180 Qubits
candidato.resumo: Insider Brief PRESS RELEASE — The National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC) at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and QuEra Computing, the leader in neutral-atom quantum computing, today announced the publication of a new study in Nature. Using Aquila, QuEra’s analog neutral-atom quantum computer, coupled with classical calculations on NERSC’s Perlmutter supercomputer, the team observed […]

texto_fonte:
Insider Brief
- QuEra Computing and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory researchers have published a Nature study using the Aquila neutral-atom quantum computer to investigate how quantum systems evolve after sudden changes.
- Experiments involving arrays of up to 180 atoms revealed long-lived prethermal states, resonant melting and a first-order dynamical phase transition without a direct equilibrium counterpart.
- The team combined Aquila experiments with classical calculations on NERSC’s Perlmutter supercomputer to validate results and investigate quantum dynamics at larger scales.
PRESS RELEASE — The National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC) at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and QuEra Computing, the leader in neutral-atom quantum computing, today announced the publication of a new study in Nature. Using Aquila, QuEra’s analog neutral-atom quantum computer, coupled with classical calculations on NERSC’s Perlmutter supercomputer, the team observed new physical phenomena, specifically how a quantum system settles after a sudden change.
The paper increases the scientific community’s understanding of processes that govern materials at the quantum scale. Classical simulation of these phenomena in large systems scales poorly, due to the fast growth of quantum entanglement with evolution time. A programmable quantum computer sidesteps this challenge by using the quantum states of the atomic qubits to model the target system and its evolution. A better understanding of how larger quantum systems evolve can inform materials science and more.
How QuEra and Berkeley Lab Worked Together
The study was co-designed by QuEra and NERSC scientists. NERSC ran exact classical calculations on Perlmutter, using QuEra’s open-source Bloqade software, for small probing systems, and those results were used to construct the quantum computer experiments. The NERSC team accessed Aquila on Amazon Braket, AWS’s quantum service.
“NERSC is focused on giving scientists access to useful computational tools. As quantum computing continues to advance, exact classical calculations are essential for validating what these machines tell us,” said Katie Klymko, NERSC Quantum Adviser. “In this work, calculations on Perlmutter gave us confidence in Aquila’s results at small scales, so we could trust the new physics it revealed at larger ones.”
The paper is the latest peer-reviewed result in a long and productive research collaboration between the Department of Energy’s National Labs and QuEra. A team from Los Alamos National Lab and QuEra published results on a new quantum error correction architecture, Transversal STAR, earlier this year.
What the Team Found
On Aquila, atomic qubits are initialized into a state in which every atom in the array starts in its lowest-energy state, a laser field switches on, the atoms evolve for a few millionths of a second, and every qubit is measured. Repeated across many settings and array shapes, from chains of up to 52 atoms to two-dimensional grids of up to 180, it produced three results.
- Long-lived intermediate states. Rather than settling smoothly, the system held distinct, stable patterns far longer than expected, a behavior known as prethermalization.
- Resonant melting. Those prethermalization patterns break down at sharp, predictable points, and the team explained quantitatively where and why.
- A two-dimensional transition with no equilibrium counterpart. In two dimensions, the system’s response changed sharply, and the change grew sharper as the array grew. The authors identify this as a first-order dynamical phase transition and find that it has no direct equilibrium correspondence.
“We usually think of phase transitions as changes in the state of matter, like water freezing into ice. But quantum matter can also undergo abrupt changes, including in how it evolves over time. Using Aquila, we discovered such a “dynamical” phase transition far from equilibrium, with no corresponding transition in the equilibrium phase diagram.” Said Milan Kornjača, Senior Quantum Scientist at QuEra and paper co-author. “This demonstrates how programmable quantum computers can reveal and explain fundamentally new physics. What excites me most is imagining what else we might discover as fault-tolerant quantum computers allow us to explore far beyond the constraints of analog computers.”
Science on Aquila
This is the latest in a substantial body of peer-reviewed research produced on Aquila, which has been available on Amazon Braket since 2022 as the first neutral-atom quantum computer on the service. Analog quantum simulation is producing published science today. The experience of building and operating a research-grade machine for the scientific community is what QuEra carries into Libra, its first fault-tolerant quantum computer, expected on Amazon Braket in 2028.
The Paper and Acknowledgements

candidato.titulo: Proton launches a privacy-first AI assistant for your PC
candidato.resumo: Proton has released its AI assistant as a standalone computer app, Lumo Desktop. The app can search for documents on your computer and retrieve information from connected services such as Google Drive and Proton Mail. Through Connections, the assistant can also work with local folders, run commands, and retrieve content from the web. Users decide for themselves which actions Lumo is allowed to perform automatically, which require approval, and which should be blocked entirely. Proton Another new feature is called Schedules, which lets you automate recurring tasks such as compiling emails every week or regularly reviewing documents and other information. Proton has also introduced Skills, reusable instructions that control how the assistant carries out specific tasks. According to the company, neither conversations nor information from connected apps is used to train AI models. Chat history is also protected by encryption designed to prevent even Proton itself from reading the content. Lumo Desktop is available to download for Windows, Linux, and macOS. The program requires a Proton account.

texto_fonte:
When Travis McGeathy’s studio, Seeker Entertainment, ran out of funding in September, its game KinForge went down with it. KinForge was an online game built in Unreal Engine 5.7 and designed to run on servers hosted by Amazon Web Services (AWS). With no one left to pay the server bill, the game became unplayable even for those few developers, including studio co-founder McGeathy, who had the code.
Then, on a whim, McGeathy pointed Anthropic’s Claude Code at the project and asked it to make KinForge playable without AWS. After four hours of mostly hands-off work he had a build that let players host their own games. Claude added support for peer-to-peer play over both the Internet and a local area network. To McGeathy’s surprise, it also added persistent save states, a feature that lets players resume a game if they’re disconnected.
Although KinForge is still built in Unreal Engine, developments like this could give companies that create game engines cause for concern. The conversion was accomplished with an agentic AI workflow that partially bypasses the elaborate, user-friendly game engine UI that many companies, including Unreal Engine creator Epic Games, have spent decades perfecting. Anthropic’s Fable 5.2, released November 9, further upped the ante. The model is capable of generating a 3D game with a custom game engine in the style of the hit Call of Duty series.
This raises a question: can game engines evolve quickly enough to keep pace with model improvements?
“We’re definitely in a world where I can just dream up software really fast. So, if Unreal Engine was static, what’s the value at the end of next year? This is why we are pivoting hard towards velocity,” says Daniel Vogel, chief operating officer at Epic Games. “I think with any fixed set of features or functionality, it can eventually be replicated. If we’re doing our job right, we’re pushing the engine and pushing the envelope forward.”
From Code to Nodes, and Back Again
Major game engines often offer developers new visual tools and workflows that help them build games while interacting with less code. Unreal Engine’s Blueprints, a graphically based system introduced in Unreal Engine 4 that lets designers script gameplay simply by wiring boxes together, is an example. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, an award-winning game from French studio Sandfall Interactive, leaned heavily on Blueprints for scripting gameplay encounters.
That should have been proof of the feature’s success. Instead, Epic will remove Blueprints in Unreal Engine 6 (UE6). Why? Blame LLMs. “AI doesn’t handle Blueprints very well,” says McGeathy. “It would much rather work with the code.”
Currently, LLMs interact with Unreal Engine primarily through a Model Context Protocol server. MCP is an open-source standard created by Anthropic that lets AI send commands to software. “It’s not actually moving the mouse,” says Ryan Barker, a gameplay and systems engineer who has worked on projects for Amazon Games and Sony Online Entertainment. “It’s sending signals to the editor that the editor understands.”
UE6 will lean into that reality by moving all code to Verse, a text-based programming language that will replace both Blueprints and Unreal Engine 5’s C++ gameplay framework. UE6 will also replace Unreal’s actor framework, which is based on object-oriented programming, with Scene Graph, which resembles an entity component system. “Typically, an ECS is a lot harder to code around,” says Barker, but ECS can provide superior game performance and result in less duplicate code. An LLM can help manage the complexity.
Verse debuted in Unreal Editor for Fortnite in 2023, while Scene Graph arrived in 2024. Verse was designed to let millions of creators run code side by side in Fortnite, so it’s strict. The compiler catches mistakes before code runs and limits what each function can do. And because Scene Graph is built on Verse, an AI can work with a game world through code. That’s different from Blueprints, which are stored as binary files that LLMs can’t read directly.
In addition to these changes, UE6 will make the engine more modular and expose its systems through an application programming interface “so that AI tooling can get at them without needing to fall back to slow computer use,” says Marcus Wassmer, the executive vice president of development at Epic Games. An internal effort that Epic calls “Python All The Things” aims to make everything in the editor scriptable. UE6 will also store more game assets as text so an LLM can edit them directly. For binary assets (non-text files) that remain, Epic is building a command-line tool that allows agents to interact with the files without loading the full UE6 interface.
The traditional Unreal Engine editor isn’t going away, but Vogel expects it will change as LLM use becomes more common. “You’re not going to move stuff visually in the editor. Those times are gone,” he says. Instead, he expects game developers will more frequently use the Unreal Engine editor to visualize “the context needed to make decisions, or make the tweaks.”
Unreal Engine 5.9 offers a glimpse at what that transition will mean in practice. Released as a developer preview on 9 November, it includes a new feature called Unreal Canvas. Vogel says it’s a collaboration feature that takes inspiration from visual workspace software like Miro. “It’s a way to make sense of the project,” says Vogel.
Why Buy an Engine When You Can Build One?
Epic Games’ goal is to keep Unreal Engine relevant in a world where AI coding tools are becoming ever-more capable. The company has the benefit of approaching the problem from a position of strength: Unreal Engine is the second most commonly used engine, after Unity Technologies’ Unity engine, and ranks first if measured by the number of games sold.
Will that be enough?
McGeathy says there can be benefits to creating an engine from scratch. “If you own the engine, you’re not reliant on a third party who could yank it out from underneath you.” However, he remains skeptical that many developers will go that route, even if AI makes it less painful. “Your goal as a game developer is to make a game. It’s not to make a game engine.”
What LLMs do change, he says, is to lower the cost of switching between game engines. McGeathy, an Unreal veteran, used Claude to start building in Godot, an open-source engine he had never touched himself. “AI made transitioning from using Unreal into Godot trivial,” he says. Barker agrees. He used an LLM to build physics test scenes in both Unreal and Godot, which let him evaluate which engine was better suited to handle a game concept.
Wassmer recognizes that AI makes it “easier [for developers using Unreal Engine] to pick up a new standard, or to convert stuff,” and says that Epic won’t attempt to block this shift. On the contrary, UE6 will remove barriers where possible. “Our explicit goal is to be able to interoperate with other ecosystems and other games,” he says.
He feels confident that, even with the aid of LLMs, building an engine from scratch carries a heavy price that most developers won’t want to pay. “You still have to burn a lot of tokens to get something of scale that is optimized and that runs across all platforms,” Wassmer says. “Would you rather spend that time and energy building something from scratch? Or would you rather use something modular, like UE6, and trim out the bits you don’t need?”
Matthew S. Smith is a freelance consumer technology journalist with 17 years of experience and the former Lead Reviews Editor at Digital Trends. An IEEE Spectrum Contributing Editor, he covers consumer tech with a focus on display innovations, artificial intelligence, and augmented reality. A vintage computing enthusiast, Matthew covers retro computers and computer games on his YouTube channel, Computer Gaming Yesterday.

candidato.titulo: Structural battery electrode enables energy storage inside curved drone legs
candidato.resumo: What if a drone's legs could do more than support its weight—and also store energy? Researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) have developed a structural battery electrode that remains stable even when fitted into curved structures, such as drone legs. By making it possible to integrate energy storage into a device's frame, the technology could help make drones and robots lighter and extend their operating times.

texto_fonte:
Structural battery electrode enables energy storage inside curved drone legs
What if a drone's legs could do more than support its weight—and also store energy? Researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) have developed a structural battery electrode that remains stable even when fitted into curved structures, such as drone legs. By making it possible to integrate energy storage into a device's frame, the technology could help make drones and robots lighter and extend their operating times.
A research team led by professor Il-Kwon Oh of the Department of Mechanical Engineering has developed a monolithically integrated lithium-sulfur (Li-S) battery cathode by growing nickel cobalt selenide (NiCo₂Se₄) nanowires directly on woven carbon cloth. Made from interwoven carbon fibers, the carbon cloth serves as a mechanically robust, flexible and electrically conductive foundation for the electrode. By growing ultrafine nanowires directly on its surface, the researchers created an electrode that combines mechanical robustness with reliable electrical conductivity.
The paper is published in the journal Advanced Composites and Hybrid Materials.
For drones and robots, maximizing energy storage while minimizing weight and space is a major engineering challenge. Conventional designs use separate batteries and structural frames, limiting opportunities to reduce overall weight and volume. Structural batteries offer a promising alternative by allowing components to both support mechanical loads and store energy. In a drone, for example, the landing legs could serve as structural supports while also functioning as part of the energy storage system.
Fitting batteries into curved structures
Turning this concept into a practical technology requires batteries that can conform to different component shapes. Drone legs and robotic frames often feature curved surfaces and hollow, tubular structures, making conventional flat battery designs difficult to integrate. The KAIST team therefore focused on developing an electrode suitable for installation within these nonplanar structures.
The researchers selected lithium-sulfur batteries, which use sulfur as the cathode material and offer the potential for high energy storage capacity at a relatively low weight. The cathode is one of a battery's two electrodes and plays a central role in the electrochemical reactions involved in charging and discharging.
Despite their advantages, lithium-sulfur batteries face several challenges. Sulfur has poor electrical conductivity, and intermediate compounds known as lithium polysulfides can dissolve and migrate away from the electrode during operation. This phenomenon can reduce battery performance by disrupting the electrochemical reactions needed for efficient energy storage.
Conventional electrode fabrication methods present an additional challenge. Active materials are typically applied to a conductive substrate as a coating, which can detach under repeated bending or mechanical stress. Such detachment can disrupt electrical pathways and compromise electrode performance.
Nanowires withstand repeated bending
To overcome these limitations, the team grew nickel cobalt selenide nanowires directly on the carbon fiber surfaces. Nanowires are extremely thin, wirelike structures measured on the nanometer scale, with one nanometer equal to one billionth of a meter. Nickel cobalt selenide, a compound containing nickel, cobalt and selenium, helps facilitate sulfur-related electrochemical reactions while also helping to capture lithium polysulfides and limit their migration.
This approach creates a tightly integrated structure in which the nanowires are firmly anchored to the carbon fibers rather than simply deposited as a separate coating. The direct connection helps maintain continuous electrical pathways, even when the electrode is bent.
The electrode demonstrated mechanical durability in bending tests. After 1,000 bending cycles at a radius of just 2.5 mm, the nanowires remained firmly attached to the carbon fiber surfaces, with no visible damage or structural collapse. The results demonstrate the electrode's ability to maintain its structural integrity under repeated bending, an important requirement for integration into tightly curved spaces.
The researchers then incorporated the electrode into a lithium-sulfur pouch cell to evaluate its feasibility for integration into various nonplanar structures. They integrated the cell into oval and square structures, as well as a drone-leg component, and successfully powered a light-emitting diode (LED). These demonstrations confirmed that the battery could supply electricity when integrated into structures with different geometries.
Reliable power under structural stress
To further evaluate its feasibility as a structural battery, the team also tested battery performance under external mechanical loads. When installed inside a cylindrical structure, the battery retained 99.8% of its initial voltage even under a load sufficient to fracture the surrounding structural frame. In a separate loading test, an LED powered by the battery remained illuminated without interruption or flickering.
The study represents an important step toward extending structural battery technology beyond the flat configurations that have dominated previous research. By demonstrating a structural battery electrode capable of operating within curved and hollow structures, the researchers have opened up new possibilities for integrating energy storage into components with complex geometries.
Looking ahead, the technology could be combined with load-bearing composite materials to create drone legs and robotic frames that provide both structural support and energy storage. Such composites typically combine materials such as carbon fibers and resins to achieve high strength at low weight. Integrating batteries into these components could make more efficient use of the limited weight and space available in drones and robots.
However, further research will be needed to determine how much weight could be saved and how significantly flight times or operating durations could be extended in practical applications.
"Drones and robots contain many curved and hollow components, so it is essential for batteries to operate reliably when integrated into these structures," said Oh. "Our study demonstrates the potential for drone legs and robotic frames to serve not only as structural components but also as energy storage systems."
More information
Jawon Ha et al., Monolithically integrated NiCo2Se4 nanowire–carbon cloth cathode scaffolds for non-planar lithium-sulfur structural-battery integration, Advanced Composites and Hybrid Materials (2026). DOI: 10.1007/s42114-026-02093-y

candidato.titulo: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
candidato.resumo: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

texto_fonte:
At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI, on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.
Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.
“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”
Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”
“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”
Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.
One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.
Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.
“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”
Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.
“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”
How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.
The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.
Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.
“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”
Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.
Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?
Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.
